A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SEC-bench and provide readable main text, figures, tables and appendices. Retained and relocated material can be matched reliably; v2 extends Appendix D and adds Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark-construction results, the CODEACT comparison, and experiments on PoC generation and vulnerability patching in Tables 1 and 3–5.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original analyses of successful PoC construction and agent trajectories in Appendices E–F.

M1.justification: The preprocessing, manager-coordinated builder/exploiter/fixer workflow, sanitizer verification and task procedures remain unchanged, as do the proposed agents' prompts. The qualified description of from-scratch PoC generation concerns capability, not a revised algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 898 candidate instances, 200 verified instances across 29 C/C++ projects, and PoC-generation and patching tasks. Appendices E–F analyze existing construction outcomes and evaluation trajectories rather than introducing new datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: CODEACT remains the comparator in Table 3. Tables 4–5 retain the same agent and model comparisons, including SWE-agent, OpenHands, Aider and the knowledge-cutoff comparisons. Appendix D.4 documents an existing baseline's prompt rather than adding a comparator.

E3.justification: The original evaluation subsets, budgets and sanitizer-based success criteria are retained. Appendices E–F add diagnostic procedures: distinguishing adaptation from from-scratch generation among 289 successful PoCs and measuring tool-use proportions by turn across SWE-agent's 200-instance trajectories. The newly stated verifier iteration cap is a disclosure, not evidence of a changed budget.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's ablation, contamination check and failure analysis, v2 adds a systematic PoC-provenance analysis, a libplist.cve-2017-7982 generation case study, and trajectory analyses for both security tasks. These substantially expand investigation of what the agents accomplish and how they behave.

E5.justification: Both versions report five SWE-agent/o3-mini runs, a 30.0% mean success rate with 7.9% standard deviation, and a Wilcoxon test with p = 0.27. The added tool-use curves describe activity frequencies; they introduce no additional uncertainty reporting or repeated-run information.

E6.justification: The existing benchmark scores remain unchanged, but substantial diagnostic findings are added. Appendix E reports only 3 from-scratch generations among 289 successful PoCs. Appendix F reports delayed editing for PoC generation, including 0.3% versus 4.5% change-tool usage at turn 10 and 2.1% versus 11.7% at turn 20, alongside new trajectory curves and a successful case study.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The revision adds empirical analyses and explanations without revising mathematical assumptions, definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same scientific claims and headline results. The introduction now explicitly states the C/C++ memory-safety scope, but that restriction was already established in v1's method and limitations sections.

C2.justification: Appendices E–F substantially expand explanations involving iteration constraints, sustained code reading, delayed editing and insufficient specialized tools, with corresponding design recommendations. From-scratch generation is more explicitly qualified as difficult and rare. Section 5 also reframes the existing sanitizer-based scope as an intentional verification tradeoff. These explanations are not validated through new budget or tool interventions.

D1.justification: Appendix D.4 supplies the integrated build/exploit/fix prompt for the existing CODEACT ablation. Appendix E identifies GPT-4o for the from-scratch successes and discloses a 75-iteration cap for each verifier agent. Existing evaluation configurations and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Related Work section are unchanged. Appendix F adds a specific relationship to prior SWE-agent research by adopting its trajectory-analysis approach and contrasting security-task behavior with its reported phases in general software-engineering tasks.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory and stylistic revisions, changes failure labels to Improper Format and Still Vulnerable, and updates the conference footer. It appends new subsections and analyses while preserving the existing narrative organization; the scientific additions do not constitute extensive rewriting of retained material.

P2.justification: The appendix gains the baseline-prompt display in Figure 9, two case-study reasoning callouts, and tool-use trajectory plots in Figures 10–11, substantially expanding the visual presentation of procedures and behavior. Figure 2 changes legend labels without changing its results; existing tables and other figures are retained.

improvement.justification: The baseline prompt improves reproducibility, while the 3-of-289 breakdown makes the construction system's reliance on existing PoCs clearer. The trajectory analyses add useful diagnostic evidence without changing the main benchmark results. These are meaningful but incremental gains: the new causal explanations about iteration budgets and tool limitations remain untested.
